claim: Netrin-1 mRNA and protein are enriched in the dorsal limb mesenchyme at the base of the mouse forelimb and hindlimb at e10.5-e11.5.
source: Comparing Netrin family ligand mRNA expression with that of Lmx1b, a dorsal limb marker (Riddle et al., 1995), revealed that at the base of the mouse forelimb and hindlimb, where LMC axons select a dorsal or ventral limb trajectory, Netrin-1 mRNA and protein were enriched in the dorsal limb mesenchyme (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A-D, comparing Netrin-1 expression with dorsal limb marker Lmx1b.

claim: Expression of β-galactosidase from an Ntn1 gene trap allele recapitulates Netrin-1 mRNA and protein distribution.
source: In addition, the expression of β-galactosidase from an Ntn1 gene trap allele (Ntn1Gt) recapitulated Netrin-1 mRNA and protein distribution (Figure 1E,F; Serafini et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1E,F and citation to Serafini et al., 1996 describing the gene trap allele.

claim: In HH st. 25 chickens, Ntn1 mRNA is confined to the dorsal limb.
source: In HH st. 25 chickens, Ntn1 mRNA was also confined to the dorsal limb (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: Unc5c is expressed in Isl1+ medial LMC neurons in mouse at e10.5-e11.5.
source: Unc5c, a repulsive Netrin-1 receptor gene, was expressed in Isl1+ medial LMC neurons (Figure 1I,J)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunostaining data shown in Figure 1I,J comparing Unc5c with medial LMC marker Isl1.

claim: Dcc and Neogenin1 are expressed by both medial and lateral LMC divisions at hindlimb and forelimb levels.
source: Dcc and Neogenin1 (Neo1), encoding attractive Netrin-1 receptors, were expressed by both LMC divisions at hindlimb and forelimb levels (Figure 1K,L; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1K,L and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unc5c protein is present in medial LMC neurons, but not in lateral LMC neurons.
source: Detection of Unc5c protein using an antibody raised against its C terminus, and Isl1 and Lhx1, confirmed that Unc5c is present in medial LMC neurons, but not in lateral LMC neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 using Unc5c antibody with LMC divisional markers.

claim: DCC is expressed by both medial and lateral LMC divisions.
source: Co-detection of DCC and Isl1 or Lhx1 proteins indicated that DCC is expressed by both LMC divisions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: DCC is present exclusively on motor axons near their spinal cord exit.
source: Examination of motor and sensory nerves near their spinal cord and dorsal root ganglion exit, before they merge into mixed sensory-motor nerves, revealed that DCC is present exclusively on motor axons, while Unc5c is expressed at high levels in motor axons with some expression in sensory axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 examining motor and sensory nerves separately.

claim: High levels of Unc5c protein are present in ventral limb nerves.
source: In the limb, high levels of Unc5c protein were present in ventral limb nerves (Figure 1M–O), consistent with its medial LMC expression
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1M-O.

claim: DCC is detected in both dorsal and ventral limb nerves.
source: while DCC was detected in both dorsal and ventral nerves (Figure 1N–O), consistent with its pan-LMC expression.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1N-O.

claim: Mouse Dscam and Unc5a are expressed in all LMC neurons.
source: Additional analysis revealed that mouse Dscam and Unc5a were expressed in all LMC neurons, while Unc5b and Unc5d were not detected in this population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mouse Unc5b and Unc5d are not detected in LMC neurons.
source: Additional analysis revealed that mouse Dscam and Unc5a were expressed in all LMC neurons, while Unc5b and Unc5d were not detected in this population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chick Unc5b and Unc5c are expressed in medial LMC neurons.
source: Chick Unc5b and Unc5c were expressed in medial LMC neurons while Unc5b and Neo1 mRNAs were found in all LMC neurons (Figure 1S–V, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1S-V and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chick Neo1 mRNA is found in all LMC neurons.
source: Chick Unc5b and Unc5c were expressed in medial LMC neurons while Unc5b and Neo1 mRNAs were found in all LMC neurons (Figure 1S–V, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1S-V and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In all mouse mutant strains examined (Ntn1Gt/Gt, Dcc-/-, Neo1Gt/Gt, Unc5c-/-, and Unc5a-/-), the specification of LMC neurons, their axon outgrowth, and Eph and ephrin expression was normal.
source: In all strains examined, the specification of LMC neurons, their axon outgrowth, and Eph and ephrin expression was normal (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; data not shown).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 examining LMC specification markers.

claim: In Dcc mutants, 9.7% of HRP-labeled neurons after ventral limb injection were medial LMC, compared with 4.4% in controls.
source: When HRP was injected into the ventral limb to detect aberrant lateral LMC axons, in Dcc mutants 9.7% of HRP-labeled neurons were medial LMC, compared with 4.4% in controls, 4.7% in Ntn1Gt/Gt and 5.6% in Unc5c-/- mice (Figure 2A–H; p=0.164, 1, and 0.748 for Dcc-/-, Ntn1Gt/Gt, and Unc5c-/- vs. controls; all values listed in Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2A-H with statistical analysis.

claim: In Ntn1Gt/Gt mice, 4.7% of HRP-labeled neurons after ventral limb injection were medial LMC.
source: When HRP was injected into the ventral limb to detect aberrant lateral LMC axons, in Dcc mutants 9.7% of HRP-labeled neurons were medial LMC, compared with 4.4% in controls, 4.7% in Ntn1Gt/Gt and 5.6% in Unc5c-/- mice (Figure 2A–H; p=0.164, 1, and 0.748 for Dcc-/-, Ntn1Gt/Gt, and Unc5c-/- vs. controls; all values listed in Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2A-H with statistical analysis.

claim: In Unc5c-/- mice, 5.6% of HRP-labeled neurons after ventral limb injection were medial LMC.
source: When HRP was injected into the ventral limb to detect aberrant lateral LMC axons, in Dcc mutants 9.7% of HRP-labeled neurons were medial LMC, compared with 4.4% in controls, 4.7% in Ntn1Gt/Gt and 5.6% in Unc5c-/- mice (Figure 2A–H; p=0.164, 1, and 0.748 for Dcc-/-, Ntn1Gt/Gt, and Unc5c-/- vs. controls; all values listed in Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2A-H with statistical analysis.

claim: Neither Neo1Gt/Gt, Dscam-/- nor Dcc-/-; Neo1Gt/Gt double mutant lateral LMC axons were found in the ventral limb at an incidence greater than that in control embryos.
source: Neither single nor double mutant lateral LMC axons were found in the ventral limb at an incidence greater than that in control embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; p=0.105, 0.537 and 0.537 for Neo1Gt/Gt, Dscam-/- and Dcc-/-; Neo1Gt/Gt vs. wild-type controls).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: Dcc, Neogenin, or Dscam are not required for in vivo lateral LMC axon guidance.
source: Thus, extensive redundancy notwithstanding, Dcc, Neogenin, or Dscam are not required for in vivo lateral LMC axon guidance.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of lateral LMC guidance defects in Neo1Gt/Gt, Dscam-/- and Dcc-/-; Neo1Gt/Gt double mutants.

claim: In wild-type mice, 3.9% of tracer-labeled LMC neurons after dorsal limb injection were medial LMC.
source: In wild-type mice, 3.9% of tracer-labeled LMC neurons were medial LMC (Figure 2K,L,S)
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2K,L,S.

claim: In Unc5c mutants, 40.4% of labeled LMC neurons after dorsal limb injection were medial LMC, corresponding to essentially random limb nerve selection.
source: whereas in Unc5c mutants, 40.4% of labeled LMC neurons were medial LMC, corresponding to essentially random limb nerve selection (Figure 2Q,R,S; p<0.001 wild-type vs. Unc5c-/-).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2Q,R,S with statistical analysis.

claim: In Ntn1Gt/Gt mice, 12.6% of labeled LMC neurons after dorsal limb injection were medial LMC, representing a significant projection error.
source: In Ntn1Gt/Gt mice, 12.6% of labeled LMC neurons were medial LMC, representing a significant projection error (Figure 2O,P,S; p<0.05 vs. wild-type).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2O,P,S with statistical analysis.

claim: Ntn1 in the dorsal limb repels medial LMC axons through Unc5c.
source: Similar incidence of misprojections in Ntn1Gt/Gt and Unc5c mutants were also observed using a medial LMC-specific transgene (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Ntn1 in the dorsal limb repels medial LMC axons through Unc5c.
evidence: Inferred from similar misprojection phenotypes in Ntn1Gt/Gt and Unc5c mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Dcc-/- mice with dorsal limb tracer injection, medial LMC neurons represented 3.3% of labeled LMC neurons, a proportion not significantly different from the 3.9% observed in controls.
source: In Dcc-/- mice with dorsal limb tracer injection, medial LMC neurons represented 3.3% of labeled LMC neurons, a proportion not significantly different from the 3.9% observed in controls (Figure 2M,N,S, p=1 vs. wild-type controls).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2M,N,S with statistical analysis.

claim: Medial LMC projections in Neo1Gt/Gt or in Dcc-/-; Neo1Gt/Gt double mutants were not different from controls.
source: Medial LMC projections in Neo1Gt/Gt or in Dcc-/-; Neo1Gt/Gt double mutants were not different from controls, and neither were they affected in Dscam-/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; p=0.537, 0.748, 0.537 for Neo1Gt/Gt, for Dcc-/-; Neo1Gt/Gt, and for Dscam-/-vs. wild-type controls, respectively)
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: Attractive Ntn1 receptors are not required for medial LMC axon guidance.
source: suggesting that attractive Ntn1 receptors are not required for medial LMC axon guidance.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of medial LMC guidance defects in Neo1Gt/Gt, Dcc-/-; Neo1Gt/Gt double mutants, and Dscam-/- mice.

claim: Lateral LMC axons identified by EphA4 expression preferentially grew on Netrin-1 stripes (75% on N, 25% on Fc stripes, p<0.001 vs. Fc/Fc controls) when confronted with Fc/N stripes.
source: However, when confronted with Fc/N stripes, lateral LMC axons preferentially grew on Netrin-1stripes (Figure 3B; 75% on N, 25% on Fc stripes p<0.001 vs. Fc/Fc controls).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: Lateral LMC axons did not show significant stripe preference when grown on Fc/Fc stripes.
source: Lateral LMC axons, identified by EphA4 expression, did not show significant stripe preference when grown on Fc/Fc stripes, with similar proportion of axons growing over either stripe (Figure 3A, 48% on Cy3-Fc vs. 52% on Fc).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LMC axon preference for Ntn1 stripes was abolished when incubated with a function-blocking antibody raised against the extracellular domain of Neo1.
source: In such experiments, LMC axon preference for Ntn1 stripes was abolished (Figure 3C, 53% on N, 47% on Fc stripes p<0.001 vs. untreated N/Fc; [Palmesino et al., 2012])
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 3C with anti-Neo1 antibody treatment and citation to Palmesino et al., 2012.

claim: Electroporation of rat Dcc expression plasmid rescued the Neo1 antibody block of lateral LMC axon preference for Netrin-1 stripes.
source: but could be rescued by electroporation of rat Dcc expression plasmid (Figure 3E; 66% on N, 34% on Fc stripes) but not with a plasmid encoding a truncated DCC (DccΔICD; Figure 3D; 48% on N, 52% on Fc stripes; p<0.001 vs. Dcc overexpression).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 3E with Dcc overexpression.

claim: A plasmid encoding truncated DCC (DccΔICD) did not rescue the Neo1 antibody block of lateral LMC axon preference for Netrin-1 stripes.
source: but could be rescued by electroporation of rat Dcc expression plasmid (Figure 3E; 66% on N, 34% on Fc stripes) but not with a plasmid encoding a truncated DCC (DccΔICD; Figure 3D; 48% on N, 52% on Fc stripes; p<0.001 vs. Dcc overexpression).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 3D with DccΔICD overexpression.

claim: Neo1 mediates lateral LMC neurite growth preference on Netrin-1.
source: These experiments show that Neo1 mediates lateral LMC neurite growth preference on Netrin-1, and that DCC is functionally equivalent.
evidence: Inferred from antibody blocking and rescue experiments showing Neo1 requirement and DCC functional equivalence.

claim: DCC is functionally equivalent to Neo1 in mediating lateral LMC neurite growth preference on Netrin-1.
source: These experiments show that Neo1 mediates lateral LMC neurite growth preference on Netrin-1, and that DCC is functionally equivalent.
evidence: Inferred from rescue of Neo1 antibody block by DCC overexpression.

claim: GFP-expressing medial LMC axons did not favor either control stripe when confronted with Fc/Fc stripes.
source: While GFP-expressing medial LMC axons did not favor either control stripe (Figure 3F; 51% on Cy3-Fc, 49% on Fc stripes)
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: When challenged with Fc/Netrin-1 stripes, medial LMC axons avoided Netrin-1 in favor of Fc (24% on N, 76% on Fc stripes, p<0.001).
source: when challenged with Fc/Netrin-1 stripes, medial LMC axons avoided Netrin-1 in favor of Fc (Figure 3G; 24% on N, 76% on Fc stripes, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 3G with statistical analysis.

claim: The repulsive effect of Netrin-1 on medial LMC neurons was abolished by siRNA targeting Unc5c.
source: This repulsive effect was abolished in medial LMC neurons electroporated with the siRNA targeting Unc5c, an effect that was rescued by expression of mouse Unc5c (Figure 3H,I; 48% on N, 52% on Fc stripes, p<0.01; 28% on N, 72% on Fc stripes, p=0.281).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 3H,I with Unc5c knockdown.

claim: Expression of mouse Unc5c rescued the effect of Unc5c siRNA on medial LMC neuron repulsion from Netrin-1.
source: This repulsive effect was abolished in medial LMC neurons electroporated with the siRNA targeting Unc5c, an effect that was rescued by expression of mouse Unc5c (Figure 3H,I; 48% on N, 52% on Fc stripes, p<0.01; 28% on N, 72% on Fc stripes, p=0.281).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 3I with Unc5c rescue.

claim: Inclusion of a function-blocking Neogenin antibody in the stripe assays did not block the repulsion of medial LMC neurites from Netrin-1.
source: Inclusion of a function-blocking Neogenin antibody in the stripe assays did not block the repulsion of medial LMC neurites from Netrin-1 (Figure 3L; 27% on N, 73% on Fc stripes, p=0.113).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 3L with anti-Neogenin antibody treatment.

claim: Netrin-1 causes repulsion of medial LMC axons through Unc5c, independently of Neogenin.
source: Thus, Netrin-1 causes repulsion of medial LMC axons through Unc5c, independently of Neogenin, providing direct evidence that Netrin-1 is a bifunctional axon guidance cue for LMC axons.
evidence: Inferred from Unc5c requirement and Neogenin independence in medial LMC repulsion from Netrin-1.

claim: Netrin-1 is a bifunctional axon guidance cue for LMC axons.
source: Thus, Netrin-1 causes repulsion of medial LMC axons through Unc5c, independently of Neogenin, providing direct evidence that Netrin-1 is a bifunctional axon guidance cue for LMC axons.
evidence: Inferred from differential responses of medial and lateral LMC axons to Netrin-1 based on receptor expression.

claim: Explanted lateral LMC neurons electroporated with an Unc5c expression plasmid avoided Netrin-1 stripes.
source: Explanted lateral LMC neurons electroporated with an Unc5c expression plasmid avoided Netrin-1 stripes.
evidence: Supported by stripe assay experiments with Unc5c overexpression in lateral LMC neurons.

claim: The repulsion of Unc5c-expressing LMC axons from Netrin-1 stripes was abolished by the expression of the Src-inhibiting kinase Csk.
source: UNC5-mediated repulsion from Netrin-1 has been shown to depend on the Src kinase (Williams et al., 2006), and indeed the repulsion of Unc5c-expressing LMC axons from Netrin-1 stripes was abolished by the expression of the Src-inhibiting kinase Csk (Figure 3J,K; 30% on N, 70% on Fc stripes vs. 59% on N, 41% on Fc stripes, p<0.001; [Imamoto and Soriano, 1993]).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 3J,K with Csk overexpression and citation to Williams et al., 2006 and Imamoto and Soriano, 1993.

claim: In embryos electroporated with [Unc5c]siRNA, 72% of GFP+ axons were present in the dorsal limb nerve, compared with 52% in GFP electroporated controls.
source: Analysis of the proportion of electroporated LMC axons entering the dorsal versus ventral limb nerves at HH st. 26 showed that in embryos electroporated with [Unc5c]siRNA, 72% of GFP+ axons were present in the dorsal limb nerve, compared with 52% in GFP electroporated controls (Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; p<0.01)
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: Chicken Unc5c is required for the fidelity of LMC trajectory choice.
source: demonstrating that chicken Unc5c is required for the fidelity of LMC trajectory choice.
evidence: Inferred from increased dorsal limb projections after Unc5c knockdown in chick.

claim: Unc5c overexpression caused 57% of GFP+ axons to select the ventral limb nerve, significantly more than the 48% in GFP-only controls (p<0.05).
source: On their own, Unc5c and EphB2-GFP caused a significantly greater fraction of GFP+ axons to select the ventral limb nerve when compared with GFP-only controls (Figure 4A,C,D; ventral limb: 48% in GFP, 57% in Unc5c/GFP, p<0.05 vs. GFP; 64% in Ephb2-GFP, p<0.01 vs. GFP).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data shown in Figure 4A,C,D with statistical analysis.

claim: EphB2-GFP overexpression caused 64% of GFP+ axons to select the ventral limb nerve, significantly more than the 48% in GFP-only controls (p<0.01).
source: On their own, Unc5c and EphB2-GFP caused a significantly greater fraction of GFP+ axons to select the ventral limb nerve when compared with GFP-only controls (Figure 4A,C,D; ventral limb: 48% in GFP, 57% in Unc5c/GFP, p<0.05 vs. GFP; 64% in Ephb2-GFP, p<0.01 vs. GFP).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data shown in Figure 4A,C,D with statistical analysis.

claim: When co-expressed, Unc5c and EphB2-GFP caused 80% of GFP+ axons to select the ventral limb nerve branch, significantly more than either alone.
source: However, when co-expressed, Unc5c and EphB2-GFP caused significantly more GFP+ axons to select the ventral limb nerve branch (Figure 4E; ventral branch: 80% in Unc5c and Ephb2-GFP, p<0.01 vs. Unc5c/GFP; p<0.01 vs. Ephb2-GFP)
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data shown in Figure 4E with statistical analysis.

claim: EphB2 and Unc5c can co-operate to guide LMC axon guidance.
source: suggesting that EphB2 and Unc5c can co-operate to guide LMC axon guidance.
evidence: Inferred from synergistic effect of co-expressing Unc5c and EphB2 on ventral limb nerve selection.

claim: EphB2 and Unc5c proteins produced from plasmids electroporated at low concentrations were approximately 30% of that induced by electroporating high plasmid concentrations.
source: We estimated that EphB2 and Unc5c proteins produced from the plasmids electroporated at low concentrations were approximately 30% of that induced by electroporating high plasmid concentrations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by protein quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of LMC axons entering the ventral limb nerve in Unc5c/GFP or Ephb-GFP embryos at low concentrations was not significantly different from controls.
source: The proportion of LMC axons entering the ventral limb nerve in such Unc5c/GFP or Ephb-GFP embryos was not significantly different from controls (Figure 4F–H; both p>0.107).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data shown in Figure 4F-H with statistical analysis.

claim: LMC axons co-expressing low levels of Ephb2-GFP and Unc5c entered the ventral limb nerve with an incidence of 74%, significantly different from controls.
source: However, LMC axons co-expressing low levels of Ephb2-GFP and Unc5c entered the ventral limb nerve with an incidence of 74%, a proportion significantly different from controls and confirmed by retrograde tracer injection into the ventral limb (Figure 4I; p<0.001; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: In vivo LMC co-operative responses to ephrin-B and Ntn1 could be synergistic in nature.
source: Together, these results suggest in vivo LMC co-operative responses to ephrin-B and Ntn1 could be synergistic in nature.
evidence: Inferred from the effect of low concentrations of Unc5c and EphB2 co-expression that individually have no effect.

claim: Medial LMC axons showed preferential growth on Fc stripes (79% on Fc, 22% on eB2) when confronted with Fc/ephrin-B2 (eB2) stripes at standard concentration.
source: To directly determine how ephrin and Netrin-1 signals co-operate in LMC axons, we took advantage of e[Isl1]::GFP-electroporated medial LMC axons' preferential growth on Fc stripes when confronted with Fc/ephrin-B2 (eB2) stripes, generated by incubation with a standard eB2 concentration (C100 eB2=10 μg/ml; Figure 5A; 79% on Fc, 22% on eB2; [Kao and Kania, 2011]).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 5A and citation to Kao and Kania, 2011.

claim: Medial LMC neurite preference for Fc stripes was significantly increased when confronted with Fc/eB2+Netrin-1 (each at C100) stripes (90% on Fc, 10% on eB2+Netrin-1, p<0.05 vs. eB2).
source: This preference was significantly increased when medial LMC neurites were confronted with Fc/eB2+Netrin-1 (each at C100) stripes mimicking the restriction of eB2 and Netrin-1 to the dorsal limb mesenchyme (Figure 5B; 90% on Fc, 10% on eB2+Netrin-1, p<0.05 vs. eB2; C100 Netrin-1 = 100 ng/ml).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: The vast majority of LMC neurons co-express both Unc5c and EphB receptors.
source: The vast majority of LMC neurons co-express both types of receptors (Kania and Jessell, 2003; Luria et al., 2008; Figure 1I–R; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; data not shown)
evidence: Supported by expression data in Figure 1I-R and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citations to Kania and Jessell, 2003 and Luria et al., 2008.

claim: Ephrins and Ntn1 can co-operatively act in individual LMC axons.
source: arguing that ephrins and Ntn1 can co-operatively act in individual LMC axons.
evidence: Inferred from co-expression of receptors in LMC neurons and synergistic responses to combined ligands.

claim: Medial LMC neurons challenged with Fc stripes versus stripes with Netrin-1 at C10 displayed no preference (48% neurites on Netrin-1; p=0.081).
source: Medial LMC neurons challenged with Fc stripes versus stripes with Netrin-1 at C50, C25, or C10 displayed no preference (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; at C10 48% neurites on Netrin-1; p=0.081)
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: Ephrin-B2 exposure at C10 resulted in no detectable preference by medial LMC neurons (45% neurites on eB2; p=0.081).
source: whereas ephrin-B2 exposure resulted in reduced preference at C50, and no detectable preference at C25, and C10 (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; at C10 45% neurites on eB2; p=0.081).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: When Netrin-1 and eB2 were presented together at C10, a striking repulsion of medial LMC axons from Netrin-1+eB2-containing stripes towards Fc stripes was observed (21% on eB2+Netrin-1 stripes at C10; p<0.001 vs. Netrin-1/Fc or eB2/Fc).
source: However, when Netrin-1 and eB2 were presented together in the same stripes, alternating with Fc stripes, we observed a striking repulsion of medial LMC axons from Netrin-1+eB2-containing stripes towards Fc stripes, at all suboptimal concentrations studied (Figure 5E; 21% on eB2+Netrin-1 stripes at C10; p<0.001 vs. Netrin-1/Fc or eB2/Fc; Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: Medial LMC axons synergistically integrate repulsion from Netrin-1 and ephrin-B2.
source: revealing that medial LMC axons synergistically integrate repulsion from Netrin-1 and ephrin-B2 (Figure 5K).
evidence: Inferred from stripe preference responses to combined subthreshold concentrations of Netrin-1 and ephrin-B2, summarized in Figure 5K.

claim: When challenged with eA5/Fc stripes, lateral LMC axons preferentially grew on Fc stripes (77% on Fc, 23% on eA5).
source: When challenged with eA5/Fc stripes, lateral LMC axons preferentially grew on Fc stripes (Figure 5F; 77% on Fc, 23% on eA5)
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: When facing eA5/Netrin-1 stripes, the preference of lateral LMC axons for non-eA5 stripes was significantly increased (87% on Fc, 13% on eA5 + Ntn1, p<0.05 vs. eA5 only).
source: but when facing eA5/Netrin-1 stripes, the preference of lateral LMC axons for non-eA5 stripes was significantly increased (Figure 5G; 87% on Fc, 13% on eA5 + Ntn1, p<0.05 vs. eA5 only).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 5G with statistical analysis.

claim: Lateral LMC neurons challenged with Fc control stripes next to stripes with either Netrin-1 or eA5 at C10 displayed no preference (at C10, 52% on Netrin-1 vs. 46% on eA5; p=0.065 vs. Netrin-1/Fc or eA5/Fc).
source: Lateral LMC neurons challenged with Fc control stripes next to stripes with either Netrin-1 or eA5 at C50 displayed a reduced preference, which was abolished at C25, and C10 (Figure 5H,I; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; at C10, 52% on Netrin-1 vs. 46% on eA5; p=0.065 vs. Netrin-1/Fc or eA5/Fc).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 5H,I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: When Netrin-1 and eA5 were presented together in alternating stripes at C10, the repulsion of lateral LMC axons from eA5 stripes was dramatically rescued (at C10 25% on eA5 and 75% on Netrin-1; p<0.001 vs. Netrin-1/Fc or eA5/Fc).
source: However, when Netrin-1 and eA5 were presented together in alternating stripes, each at C50, C25, and C10, the repulsion of lateral LMC axons from eA5 stripes was dramatically rescued (Figure 5J; at C10 25% on eA5 and 75% on Netrin-1; p<0.001 vs. Netrin-1/Fc or eA5/Fc).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 5J with statistical analysis.

claim: Lateral LMC axons integrate attractive and repulsive responses to Ntn1 and eA5, respectively, in a synergistic manner.
source: These data are summarized in a fidelity index plot in Figure 5L and reveal that lateral LMC axons integrate attractive and repulsive responses to Ntn1 and eA5, respectively, in a synergistic manner.
evidence: Inferred from stripe preference responses to combined subthreshold concentrations of Netrin-1 and ephrin-A5, summarized in Figure 5L.

claim: Lateral and medial LMC growth cones synergistically integrate opposing and congruent Netrin and ephrin signals.
source: Together, these experiments reveal that lateral and medial LMC growth cones synergistically integrate opposing and congruent Netrin and ephrin signals.
evidence: Inferred from synergistic responses observed in both lateral and medial LMC neurons to combined Netrin and ephrin signals.

claim: A high concentration of eB2 (10 μg/ml) elicited a significant increase in medial LMC growth cone collapse over controls (62% vs. 18% Fc-treated; p=0.008).
source: A high concentration of eB2 (10 μg/ml) elicited a significant increase in collapse over controls (Figure 6A–C; 62% vs. 18% Fc-treated; p=0.008)
evidence: Supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 6A-C with statistical analysis.

claim: Exposure to lower eB2 (1 μg/ml) or Netrin-1 (300 ng/ml) concentrations resulted in negligible medial LMC growth cone collapse (p=0.194 and p=0.412, respectively, vs. Fc).
source: and exposure to lower eB2 (1 μg/ml) or Netrin-1 (300 ng/ml) concentrations resulted in negligible collapse (p=0.194 and p=0.412, respectively, vs. Fc).
evidence: Supported by growth cone collapse assay data with statistical analysis.

claim: Exposure of medial LMC growth cones to a mix of eB2 and Netrin-1 at low concentrations resulted in 73% collapse, significantly different from either ligand alone, or Fc controls (p< 0.029).
source: Exposure of medial LMC growth cones to a mix of eB2 and Netrin-1 at low concentrations resulted in 73% collapse, significantly different from either ligand alone, or Fc controls (Figure 6B; p< 0.029)
evidence: Supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 6B with statistical analysis.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying ephrin-B2- Netrin-1 synergy can operate over a relatively short timescale.
source: suggesting that the molecular mechanisms underlying ephrin-B2- Netrin-1 synergy can operate over a relatively short timescale.
evidence: Inferred from synergistic growth cone collapse observed after 30 minutes of ligand exposure.

claim: All treatments (Fc, eB2, Netrin-1, and both eB2 and Netrin-1) result in the same receptor protein signal levels in LMC growth cones.
source: In all cases, EphB and Unc5c expression levels remained essentially unchanged in LMC growth cones (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immunodetection of Unc5c and EphB2 revealed a high incidence of Unc5c- and EphB-containing membrane patches, whose number and size were constant under all conditions.
source: However, immunodetection of Unc5c and EphB2 revealed a high incidence of Unc5c- and EphB-containing membrane patches, whose number and size were constant under all conditions (Figure 6D–J, p>0.05; Figure 6—figure supplement 1, data not shown [Costes et al., 2004])
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6D-J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, with citation to Costes et al., 2004.

claim: There is existence of ephrin-Netrin receptor complexes in discrete cell membrane domains of the growth cone.
source: suggesting the existence of ephrin-Netrin receptor complexes in discrete cell membrane domains of the growth cone.
evidence: Inferred from co-localization of Unc5c and EphB2 in membrane patches.

claim: The anti-GFP antibody precipitated Unc5c when Unc5c-Myc was co-expressed with EphB2-GFP but not with EphA3-GFP or in the absence of EphB2-GFP.
source: We found that the anti-GFP antibody precipitated Unc5c when Unc5c-Myc was co-expressed with EphB2-GFP but not with EphA3-GFP or in the absence of EphB2-GFP (Figure 6K).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: The association between EphB2-GFP and Unc5c-Myc was increased ~22 times after pre-incubation with eB2-Fc (p<0.01).
source: We found that the association between EphB2-GFP and Unc5c-Myc was increased ~22 times after pre-incubation with eB2-Fc (Figure 6L and Figure 6—figure supplement 1N, p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6L and Figure 6—figure supplement 1N with statistical analysis.

claim: The EphB2-Unc5c association was induced in a ligand-specific manner, since incubations with Netrin-1, eA3-Fc or Fc did not stimulate Netrin-ephrin receptor interactions.
source: This association was induced in a ligand-specific manner, since incubations with Netrin-1, eA3-Fc or Fc did not stimulate Netrin-ephrin receptor interactions (Figure 6L).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6L with different ligand treatments.

claim: Exposure to combined Netrin-1 and eB2-Fc increased EphB2-GFP–Unc5c interactions to a similar extent as eB2-Fc alone.
source: Exposure to combined Netrin-1 and eB2-Fc increased EphB2-GFP–Unc5c interactions to a similar extent as eB2-Fc alone (Figure 6L and Figure 6—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6L and Figure 6—figure supplement 1N.

claim: A basal association between EphB2 and Unc5c is increased by ephrin-B2.
source: Thus, a basal association between EphB2 and Unc5c is increased by ephrin-B2.
evidence: Inferred from ligand-dependent increase in EphB2-Unc5c co-immunoprecipitation.

claim: The loss of EphB2 kinase function reduced the extent of Unc5c-EphB2 interaction by ~67% when compared with the wild-type EphB2-GFP (p<0.01).
source: We found that the loss of kinase function reduced the extent of interaction by ~67% when compared with the wild-type EphB2-GFP (Figure 6M, Figure 6—figure supplement 1O, p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6M and Figure 6—figure supplement 1O with statistical analysis.

claim: Exposure to both eB2 and Netrin-1 generated a significant increase of ~23% in tyrosine phosphorylation of EphB2 when compared with ephrin-B2 alone (p<0.02).
source: Exposure to both eB2 and Netrin-1 generated a significant increase of ~23% in tyrosine phosphorylation of EphB2 when compared with ephrin-B2 alone (Figure 6N, p<0.02).
evidence: Supported by phospho-EphB2 detection data shown in Figure 6N with statistical analysis.

claim: Concomitant stimulation with ephrin-B2 and Netrin-1 induces the formation of an EphB2-Unc5c receptor complex and increases EphB2 tyrosine phosphorylation levels.
source: Together, our biochemical experiments indicate that concomitant stimulation with ephrin-B2 and Netrin-1 induces the formation of an EphB2-Unc5c receptor complex and increases EphB2 tyrosine phosphorylation levels, commensurate with elevated biological activity.
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation and phosphorylation data showing ligand-dependent complex formation and increased EphB2 phosphorylation.

claim: SFKs are not required for the formation of the Unc5c-EphB2 complex.
source: First, we observed that SFKs were not required for the formation of the Unc5c-EphB2 complex (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as an observation from experiments not shown.

claim: After 15 min, increasing doses of eB2 generated increased LMC growth cone pSFK signal that coincided with EphB receptor clusters.
source: After 15 min, following ligand application but before completion of growth cone collapse, increasing doses of eB2 generated increased LMC growth cone pSFK signal that coincided with EphB receptor clusters, while Netrin-1 alone failed to induce pSFK, when compared with Fc treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; data not shown).
evidence: Supported by pSFK immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Netrin-1 alone failed to induce pSFK in LMC growth cones after 15 min, when compared with Fc treatment.
source: After 15 min, following ligand application but before completion of growth cone collapse, increasing doses of eB2 generated increased LMC growth cone pSFK signal that coincided with EphB receptor clusters, while Netrin-1 alone failed to induce pSFK, when compared with Fc treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; data not shown).
evidence: Supported by pSFK immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: After 30 min of simultaneous exposure to eB2 and Netrin-1, significantly higher levels of pSFK were seen in collapsing LMC growth cones when compared with those exposed to either ligand alone or Fc (p<0.01).
source: After 30 min of simultaneous exposure to eB2 and Netrin-1, significantly higher levels of pSFK were seen in collapsing LMC growth cones when compared with those exposed to either ligand alone or Fc (Figure 7A–F,G; p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by pSFK immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 7A-F,G with statistical analysis.

claim: Simultaneous exposure to eB2 and Netrin-1 might result in prolonged elevation of pSFK levels.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that simultaneous exposure to eB2 and Netrin-1 might result in prolonged elevation of pSFK levels.
evidence: Inferred from higher pSFK levels at 30 min with combined ligands compared to individual ligands.

claim: SU6656 completely blocked the collapse of LMC growth cones evoked by ephrin-B2.
source: SU6656, an SFK inhibitor, completely blocked the collapse of LMC growth cones evoked by ephrin-B2 but only attenuated by 8% the collapse caused by simultaneous eB2 and Netrin-1 application (Figure 7H–I; p<0.05; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; data not shown; Blake et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 7H-I and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 with SU6656 treatment, and citation to Blake et al., 2000.

claim: SU6656 only attenuated by 8% the collapse caused by simultaneous eB2 and Netrin-1 application (p<0.05).
source: SU6656, an SFK inhibitor, completely blocked the collapse of LMC growth cones evoked by ephrin-B2 but only attenuated by 8% the collapse caused by simultaneous eB2 and Netrin-1 application (Figure 7H–I; p<0.05; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; data not shown; Blake et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 7H-I and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 with SU6656 treatment, and citation to Blake et al., 2000.

claim: The combination of SU6656 with eB2 and Netrin-1 at 1/10th of standard concentrations resulted in a 19% attenuation of synergistic collapse (p<0.001).
source: The combination of SU6656 with eB2 and Netrin-1 at 1/10th and 1/30th of the above concentrations, resulted in a 19% and 29% attenuation of synergistic collapse, respectively (Figure 7I, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 7I with statistical analysis.

claim: The combination of SU6656 with eB2 and Netrin-1 at 1/30th of standard concentrations resulted in a 29% attenuation of synergistic collapse (p<0.001).
source: The combination of SU6656 with eB2 and Netrin-1 at 1/10th and 1/30th of the above concentrations, resulted in a 19% and 29% attenuation of synergistic collapse, respectively (Figure 7I, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 7I with statistical analysis.

claim: Medial LMC neuron over-expression of Csk completely blocked responses to Fc/N and Fc/eB2 stripes at C100 (p<0.01).
source: In stripe assays, medial LMC neuron over-expression of Csk, an inhibitory kinase of Src (Imamoto and Soriano, 1993), completely blocked responses to Fc/N and Fc/eB2 stripes at C100 (Figure 7J–M, p<0.01)
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 7J-M with Csk overexpression and citation to Imamoto and Soriano, 1993.

claim: Csk overexpression attenuated the preference elicited by Fc/N+eB2 stripes at C100 concentration by 57% (p<0.01).
source: while the preference elicited by Fc/N+eB2 stripes at C100 concentration was attenuated by 57% (Figure 7N–O, p<0.01)
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 7N-O with statistical analysis.

claim: Csk overexpression reduced the preference elicited by Fc/N+eB2 stripes at C10 by 87% (p<0.001).
source: and it was reduced by 87% when challenged with Fc/N+eB2 stripes at C10 (Figure 7P–Q; p<0.001; detailed quantification: Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by stripe assay data shown in Figure 7P-Q with statistical analysis.

claim: SFK activation is a key step in the integration of ephrin-B2 and Netrin-1 signaling that leads to elevated repulsion of LMC growth cones.
source: Together, these results indicate that SFK activation is a key step in the integration of ephrin-B2 and Netrin-1 signaling that leads to elevated repulsion of LMC growth cones.
evidence: Inferred from SFK inhibitor and Csk overexpression experiments showing requirement for synergistic responses.

claim: Acting through its attractive and repulsive receptors, Netrin-1 guides spinal motor axons in the limb.
source: Our genetic in vivo and in vitro assays argue that 1. acting through its attractive and repulsive receptors, Netrin-1 guides spinal motor axons in the limb
evidence: Summary statement based on genetic and in vitro experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Netrin-1 and A-class and B-class ephrins synergize in attractive-repulsive (opposing) and repulsive-repulsive (congruent) modes to guide motor axons.
source: 2. Netrin-1 and A-class and B-class ephrins synergize in attractive-repulsive (opposing) and repulsive-repulsive (congruent) modes to guide motor axons
evidence: Summary statement based on stripe assay experiments showing synergistic integration.

claim: Unc5c and EphB receptors form an ephrin-B ligand-dependent and Eph tyrosine kinase-dependent complex.
source: 3. Unc5c and EphB receptors form an ephrin-B ligand-dependent and Eph tyrosine kinase-dependent complex
evidence: Summary statement based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Congruent synergy involves the potentiation of common effectors of ephrin and Netrin signaling pathways such as SFKs.
source: 4. congruent synergy involves the potentiation of common effectors of ephrin and Netrin signaling pathways such as SFKs.
evidence: Summary statement based on pSFK analysis and SFK inhibitor experiments.

claim: Netrin-1 likely functions as a contact-dependent axon guidance cue for LMC growth cones at the limb nerve bifurcation abutting the Netrin-1 expression domain.
source: Additionally, since Netrin-1 protein localization in the limb matches closely that of its mRNA, Netrin-1 likely functions as a contact-dependent axon guidance cue for LMC growth cones at the limb nerve bifurcation abutting the Netrin-1 expression domain.
evidence: Inferred from Netrin-1 protein localization matching mRNA expression and in vitro responses to immobilized Netrin-1.

claim: DCC is dispensable for Unc5c-mediated medial LMC guidance.
source: One corollary of this, based on non-vertebrate models of Netrin repulsion (Keleman and Dickson, 2001), would be the lack of requirement for attractive Netrin receptors for short range Unc5c-mediated LMC axon guidance, in agreement with our genetic experiments showing that DCC is dispensable for Unc5c-mediated medial LMC guidance.
evidence: Inferred from genetic experiments showing normal medial LMC guidance in Dcc mutants, with citation to Keleman and Dickson, 2001.

claim: Residual Netrin-1 protein in Ntn1 mutants could account for the weaker misprojection phenotype compared to Unc5c mutants.
source: In addition, the hypomorphic nature of the Ntn1Gt mutation (Serafini et al., 1996), with residual Netrin-1 protein guiding some medial LMC axons in Ntn1 mutants, could account for the weaker misprojection phenotype.
evidence: Speculative explanation for phenotypic differences between Ntn1 and Unc5c mutants, with citation to Serafini et al., 1996.

claim: Neo1 function is required for Netrin-1-mediated axon guidance.
source: Our in vitro antibody blocking experiments directly demonstrate that Neo1 function is required for Netrin-1-mediated axon guidance and the functional equivalence of DCC and Neo1.
evidence: Inferred from antibody blocking experiments showing loss of Netrin-1 preference.

claim: The intracellular effectors of Netrin-1:DCC attraction signaling are present in chicken lateral LMC neurons.
source: The rescue of Neo1 antibody block by DCC expression also implies that the intracellular effectors of Netrin-1:DCC attraction signaling are present in chicken lateral LMC neurons.
evidence: Inferred from functional rescue of Neo1 block by DCC overexpression.

claim: In vivo, attractive Netrin-1 receptors are dispensable for the fidelity of lateral LMC axon guidance.
source: Contrary to our in vitro experiments where Neo1 loss of function results in loss of growth preference on Netrin-1, genetic loss of DCC and nearly all of Neo1, or Dscam, does not lead to any lateral LMC guidance defects, suggesting that in vivo, attractive Netrin-1 receptors are dispensable for the fidelity of lateral LMC axon guidance.
evidence: Inferred from lack of lateral LMC guidance defects in Dcc, Neo1, and Dscam mutants.

claim: Contrasting modes of synergistic integration occur in related populations of spinal motor neurons.
source: Thus, contrasting modes of synergistic integration occur in related populations of spinal motor neurons, possibly reflecting the evolutionary advantage of axon guidance synergy.
evidence: Inferred from observation of both opposing and congruent synergistic integration in lateral and medial LMC neurons.

claim: A considerable fraction of EphB and Unc5c receptors on the surface of medial LMC growth cones is found in the same membrane compartment.
source: As a first step of our model, independent of ligands, a considerable fraction of EphB and Unc5c receptors on the surface of medial LMC growth cones is apparently found in the same membrane compartment, contrasting the non-overlapping distribution of some ephrins and Eph receptors (Marquardt et al., 2005).
evidence: Inferred from co-localization data and citation to Marquardt et al., 2005.

claim: Membrane compartment co-existence of EphB and Unc5c might facilitate the formation of EphB2-Unc5c complexes following the addition of ephrin-B2.
source: Such membrane compartment co-existence might facilitate the formation of EphB2-Unc5c complexes following the addition of ephrin-B2, as detected in our biochemical assays.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on co-localization and co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Netrin-1 presence increased EphB2 tyrosine-phosphorylation, a correlate of Eph receptor activation required for many of its functions.
source: In support of the second possibility, Netrin-1 presence increased EphB2 tyrosine-phosphorylation, a correlate of Eph receptor activation required for many of its functions (Zisch et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by phospho-EphB2 detection data and citation to Zisch et al., 1998.

claim: The coincidence of ephrin-B2 and Netrin-1 resulted in prolonged activating phosphorylation of SFKs when compared with that induced by ephrin-B2 alone.
source: We also found that the coincidence of ephrin-B2 and Netrin-1 resulted in prolonged activating phosphorylation of SFKs when compared with that induced by ephrin-B2 alone, and that SFK function is required in LMC neurons for ephrin-B2-Ntn1 synergistic responses.
evidence: Supported by pSFK detection and SFK inhibitor experiments.

claim: SFK function is required in LMC neurons for ephrin-B2-Ntn1 synergistic responses.
source: We also found that the coincidence of ephrin-B2 and Netrin-1 resulted in prolonged activating phosphorylation of SFKs when compared with that induced by ephrin-B2 alone, and that SFK function is required in LMC neurons for ephrin-B2-Ntn1 synergistic responses.
evidence: Supported by SFK inhibitor and Csk overexpression experiments.

claim: Src mutation abolishes the fidelity of medial LMC limb nerve selection.
source: Thus, since Src mutation abolishes the fidelity of medial LMC limb nerve selection (Kao et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2004)
evidence: Cited from previous studies by Kao et al., 2009 and Liu et al., 2004.

claim: The second step of ephrin-Netrin synergy might entail increased EphB2 and Src kinase activity leading to more intense activation of common signaling pathways.
source: the second step might entail increased EphB2 and Src kinase activity leading to more intense activation of common signaling pathways.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on increased EphB2 phosphorylation and SFK activation data.

claim: Additional, non-SFK mechanisms integrating Netrin-ephrin signaling may exist.
source: The fact that SFK inhibitors could not totally block repulsive growth cone responses upon Netrin-1-ephrin-B2 stimulation raises the interesting possibility that additional, non-SFK mechanisms integrating Netrin-ephrin signaling exist.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on incomplete block of synergistic responses by SFK inhibitors.

claim: In EphB1 and EphB3 mutants many medial LMC axons can be labeled from dorsal limb muscles.
source: Furthermore, the genetic observation that in EphB1 and EphB3 mutants many medial LMC axons can be labeled from dorsal limb muscles (Luria et al., 2008)
evidence: Cited from previous study by Luria et al., 2008.
